Hi! I'm Michiru, your guide. This is your first story here, so how about a one-minute tour of how a chat works?
Every story starts with an opening scene, like this one. Read it, then it's your turn to step in.
This story has more than one opening. Use the arrows to browse them and pick the one you like before you start.

This box is where you write what your character says or does. Plain text works fine. If you like, put speech in "quotes" and actions in *asterisks*, the two little buttons under the box do that for you. Both are optional.
Stuck for ideas? The sparkle button asks the story for five possible next moves. Pick one and it fills the box for you.
Your turn! Type anything you like, a hello or something bold, then tap the send button.
Type a message and send it
Now the story writes back. Sit tight and wait for the reply to finish before your next move.
Wait for the reply to finish
And there's your reply! Every turn works like this: you write, the story answers. Now let me show you the buttons under it.
Continue moves the story forward without you writing anything. Great when you just want to see what happens next.
The pencil hides the writing box when you don't need it. Take a Turn brings it back whenever you want to speak.
Not happy with a reply? Retry rolls a new version of it. Type instructions first and it becomes a retry with directions.
Erase removes the latest message, so you can take back a turn and try something else.
Every message has its own menu too. Tap the newest message to open it.
Info shows the details of this message: which model wrote it, how many tokens it used and what it cost.
Edit lets you rewrite the text of a message, yours or the story's. Handy for fixing a name or nudging a scene.
Delete removes this message from the story for good.
Branch starts a second timeline from this exact point. This one stays intact, so you can try a different path and come back later.
Copy puts the message text on your clipboard.
Save bookmarks the message so you can jump back to it later.
This row turns the scene into more than words: narration, illustrations, manga, a visual novel, music or a video clip. These cost Mana, so try them once you're settled in.
Up top: the eye keeps only the newest message in focus, the magnifier searches the chat, and the gear opens the settings. Tap the gear now.
This card is the model, the brain writing your story. Tap it to pick another one. Cheaper models cost less Mana per turn, stronger ones write better and remember more.
Text is measured in tokens, roughly three quarters of a word each. Every turn, the whole story so far is sent to the model, so a longer chat costs a bit more Mana per turn.
The context limit is how much the model can read at once. When your story grows past it, the oldest messages fall out of its view. The bar here shows how full it is.

Summaries fix that. This section turns older messages into chapters, and chapters into arcs. The model reads the short version instead, so it remembers the plot and each turn costs less. Use it when your story gets long.
That's everything you need. The rest you'll discover as you play. Go back to your story and have fun! You can replay this tour anytime from the UI/UX tab.

These instructions guide the AI that picks a character foreground, background, illustration and music for each chat message. Customize them to fit your story's tone, this storyline only.

The available lists are filled into {{charVar}}, {{bgVar}}, {{illVar}} and {{musicVar}} automatically (or appended at the end if you remove them). The current location, the currently playing track, recently shown illustrations, the player's message, the AI's reply, and the response format are always added by the system, your text controls only the selection rules.

After every AI message, the picker reads it and chooses ONE character foreground and ONE background from this storyline's gallery (images and videos with "Select by AI" enabled). If a soundtrack is attached, it also decides which track should be playing, or stops the music.
Along with your instructions, it sees option lists built from each image's name and description, and each soundtrack track with your Music AI notes. For example:

- [image 1 Aria] - Aria smiling warmly, hands clasped / - [image 2 Aria] - Aria crying, devastated / - [image 3 Kade] - Kade smirking confidently (You/Player) /  / - [image 1] - A rainy graveyard at dusk / - [image 2] - A sunny festival street /  / - [track 1] - "Gentle Meadow": calm ambience, play by default / - [track 2] - "Steel and Fury": battle scenes /  / - [art 1] - Their first kiss under the fireworks

It must answer with the exact bracketed keys (e.g. [image 2 Aria], [track 2], or "stop" for silence). That format is enforced automatically, so your prompts only shape HOW it chooses, never the output format.

The picker can only tell foregrounds apart by their descriptions, and tracks by their Music AI notes. Give every image a distinct, emotion-labeled description and every track a clear when-to-play note. That matters more than the prompts themselves.

By default it runs on {{model}} (fallback: {{fallback}}), you can pick a different model above. These are fast, lightweight models: keep instructions simple and direct; long clever prompts work worse, and your prompt counts toward every message's cost.

What can the codex be used for?

World lore: history, locations, factions, characters' secrets, magic rules. The AI only sees each entry's one-line description until the story touches it, then reads the full text: so heavy lore costs nothing until it matters.

Living records: turn on "AI can update" for quest logs, relationship trackers, journals, faction reputation. Give the entry a starting format and the AI keeps it updated as the story progresses. Add "Auto expand on read" to make it a visible tracker: the card shows the latest version whenever the AI reads or updates it.
Designed reveals: turn on "Auto expand on read" for letters, posters, prophecies or documents you want shown to the player as a card at the dramatic moment the AI reads them.

Twists and secrets: "Unlockable" keeps an entry locked in the player's codex browser until the AI reads it, then it unlocks as a discovery. "Hidden (AI only)" keeps the content AI-only forever: the player only ever sees the entry's title (on read cards and as a sealed row in the codex), never its text: secret rules, scripted events, and notes for the AI alone. "Read once" is for one-time EVENTS and achievements: an ambush, a betrayal, an achievement earned, a ritual that fires when the story reaches it: the AI consumes it a single time per chat and it never triggers again. "Spoiler" keeps an unlocked entry's text behind a warning in the player's codex, for content that telegraphs outcomes.

The description is what tells the AI WHEN to read an entry: write it like a trigger: "Read when the party approaches the northern ruins". Anything the AI must always know belongs in the main prompt instead.

AI instructions: content does not have to be lore: it can be directives for the AI itself. How a battle system works in this dungeon, how a character must behave once their secret is out, rules for a specific scene. The AI reads and follows them exactly when the description says to.
